From Army Psychiatrist to Death Row: The Final Chapter of the Nidal Hasan Case


The United States is preparing to turn a particularly dark page in its military history. Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist of Palestinian descent, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3, 2026, at Fort Hood, Texas. Unless the courts intervene, the execution would be the first of a U.S. service member since 1961.

The location gives the case an especially chilling dimension. It was at Fort Hood, on November 5, 2009, that Hasan opened fire inside a military medical facility. Within minutes, 13 people were killed and 32 others were wounded. Most of the victims were service members on the base preparing for overseas deployments.

At the time, Hasan was himself an Army officer and psychiatrist. His role included providing psychological care to soldiers dealing with the effects of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The contrast between his position as a military doctor and his transformation into the perpetrator of a deadly shooting profoundly shocked the American public.

In 2013, following a court-martial, Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder. He was sentenced to death.

Hasan chose to represent himself during the trial and largely did not dispute the facts presented against him. His conviction was followed, however, by years of legal proceedings that delayed the final resolution of the case.

That changed recently when U.S. authorities moved forward with plans to carry out the execution.

“The fact that the president has approved the execution does not necessarily mean it will take place on the scheduled date,” 
said Mike Mulligan, a former military prosecutor involved in the case. According to Mulligan, further legal challenges could still delay the execution.

Geoffrey Corn, a former Army lieutenant colonel and military law expert, has also emphasized the complexity of the process. Under the U.S. military justice system, a death sentence must clear multiple legal stages before it can actually be carried out. Setting an execution date, therefore, does not mean the outcome is legally guaranteed.

But the Hasan case has already brought the issue of military capital punishment back into the national spotlight.

The decision to use a firing squad adds another extraordinary dimension to the case. The method is exceedingly rare in the United States today and belongs largely to an earlier era of military justice. The last U.S. service member to be executed was put to death in 1961.

If the sentence is carried out, Hasan would become the first U.S. service member executed in 65 years. He could also become the first person in the modern era of the U.S. military to be put to death by firing squad.

The symbolism is difficult to ignore. Fort Hood would not simply remain the site of the 2009 shooting that claimed 13 lives. The base could also become the setting for the final chapter of a case that has stretched across nearly 17 years.

The case, however, remains surrounded by uncertainty. Hasan’s attorneys can still ask the courts to halt or postpone the execution. A judicial ruling could therefore alter the currently announced schedule.

For the victims’ families, the prospect comes after more than a decade of waiting. For the U.S. military, it raises a historic question: after 65 years without a military execution, is America preparing to revive a practice many believed belonged to the past?

The countdown is now underway.

On December 3, 2026, at Fort Hood, Nidal Malik Hasan could be led before a firing squad. Unless the courts intervene, the former Army psychiatrist would become the first member of the U.S. armed forces executed since 1961.

A case born in blood nearly 17 years ago could thus reach its final chapter at the very place where it began.
